findings.title: Per-chunk session-bounds query adds a DB round trip to every chunk of every symbol
findings.description: The new `fetch_session_bounds(bounds_conn, symbol, chunk_start, chunk_end)` call runs for every fetched chunk, for every symbol, in both phases. With ~13,000 symbols and multiple chunks per symbol per pass this is thousands of extra queries per pass, each opening a fresh pooled connection (`pool.connection()`), on top of the provider request. The session calendar is already loaded per symbol elsewhere in the loop (the seed path calls `fetch_sessions`/`fetch_session_bounds` inside `compute_missing_minute_sessions`); caching the bounds per symbol for the pass, or restricting the query to the sessions actually intersecting the chunk, would remove the repeated round trip. This is a hot path that scales with the universe, so it should be bounded rather than per-chunk.

findings.title: A chunk judged PARTIAL keeps the gap row but the retry loop can spin on it
findings.description: When `judge_chunk_by_sessions` returns PARTIAL because the provider has not yet published the session, `_advance_minute_gap` maps PARTIAL to `FetchStatus.UNKNOWN` (via `outcome_to_fetch_status`), which keeps the row actionable and increments `attempt_count`. The next chunk selection re-picks the same newest actionable gap (`ORDER BY gap_end DESC`), so the same unpublished session is re-requested immediately, burning quota until `MAX_RETRY_COUNT` promotes it to `RETRY_EXHAUSTED` — a terminal status that then requires the repair script to clear. The previous behaviour deleted the row (the bug being fixed) but at least did not burn the allowance in a tight loop. The new path needs an explicit backoff or a distinct "provider has not published" status so the retry does not become a quota spin; note the comment says "row kept" but does not say what stops the immediate re-request.

findings.title: `cagg_freshness_for_session` compares a refresh timestamp with `created_at`, but `created_at` is not part of the cagg's read window
findings.description: The probe reads `max(created_at)` from `minute_ohlcv` over the session window and compares it with the cagg policy's `last_successful_finish`. Two problems: (1) `minute_ohlcv.created_at` defaults to `NOW()` at insert, but rows inserted by the COPY/ON CONFLICT path are only written when the bar is new — so a re-fetch of an already-present bar does not move `created_at`, meaning the probe can report "fresh" while the cagg is genuinely behind. (2) The `last_successful_finish` of *any* refresh job for the cagg is used, including a run whose window did not cover the session at all, so a recent-but-irrelevant refresh reads as fresh. The `cagg_freshness.assert_cagg_fresh` module already exists and encodes the project's D3 rule ("indeterminate freshness is stale", never a pass); this new probe duplicates that logic in a second place with a weaker comparison, which the AGENTS.md "one value, one source" and "do not duplicate logic" rules discourage. Consider deriving the verdict from `assert_cagg_fresh` plus a content check instead.

findings.title: The WAIT verdict is indistinguishable from FAIL to the health check and the cutover
findings.description: `run_verify` prints `[WAIT]` and returns `False`, which the repair CLI maps to `EXIT_REFUSED` (2). The cutover's `_verify_when_fresh` detects the `[WAIT]` literal in the text and re-polls, but `mt data health` does not run `--verify` at all, and any other consumer of the repair script's exit code cannot distinguish "not yet measurable" from "measured and failed". A WAIT that ends up as a generic non-zero exit is exactly the kind of silent-ish failure the project rules forbid. A distinct exit code (or a structured verdict) would let the cutover and any operator distinguish the two.

findings.title: `cagg_freshness_for_session` can report stale for a session whose bars were never written
findings.description: `newest_bar_written` is `max(created_at)` over `minute_ohlcv` for the session window, and `CaggFreshness.stale` is False only when `newest_bar_written is None`. A judged session with genuinely zero bars (the very failure the mass check exists to catch) yields `newest_bar_written = None` → not stale → the mass read proceeds and correctly reports FAIL. That path is fine, but the inverse is not: a session whose bars were written *before* the last refresh but which the cagg's `end_offset` deliberately excludes (the 4-hour cagg has `end_offset => 4 hours`, so the newest bucket is never materialized while open) will read as fresh while the mass read legitimately reports fewer bars than exist. The probe's premise — "a bar landed after the last refresh" ⟺ "the cagg has not materialized it" — is not equivalent to the cagg's own policy semantics.

findings.title: Sudoers wildcards are broader than the file's own comment claims
findings.description: The header says "Exactly the commands those scripts issue, nothing wider", but `MT_UNITS` grants `systemctl stop mt-*`, `start mt-*`, `restart mt-*` — that wildcard covers every `mt-*` unit, including `mt-serve.service` (the API server) and any future unit, and `restart mt-*` allows taking the serving layer down. `MT_RUN` grants `/usr/local/bin/mt-run *`, which reaches `mt-run <anything>` → the production `mt` CLI with root (`run_production_mt` execs `/opt/manta-trading/.venv/bin/mt`), i.e. arbitrary production database operations as root. `MT_INSTALL` names an absolute path under `/home/manta/...` while the installer's `ProtectHome`/unit assumptions are elsewhere — and the script actually runs the installer from the checkout, so the path is operator-specific and will not match on other hosts. These are broad grants for a "limited root" file; the comment's claim is inaccurate, and the grants should be narrowed (specific unit names, specific `mt-run` subcommands) or the comment corrected to describe what is actually granted.

findings.title: The cutover log is written into the repository tree, not a gitignored location
findings.description: `start_log(NOTES_DIR / f"921-cutover-{...}.log")` writes under `project-documents/user/notes/`, which is inside the repo. The cutover runs with root privileges on the production host and writes a file the operator's checkout will then see as an untracked modification — the same class of problem `deploy/install-production.sh` guards against with its dirty-tree check ("existing checkout has local modifications — aborting untouched"). There is no `.gitignore` entry for `*.log` under that directory (the global `*.log` ignore is in the standard Python block, so it may be covered, but the notes directory is a documents tree, not a log tree). Consider writing the narration outside the checkout (e.g. `/var/log/manta-trading/`) or adding an explicit ignore entry.

findings.title: `judge_chunk_by_sessions` computes `judged` and then recomputes the same set inside `sessions_without_bars`
findings.description: `judge_chunk_by_sessions` builds `judged = [open_ for open_, close in session_bounds.items() if close <= chunk_end]` and then calls `sessions_without_bars`, which re-derives the same filter internally. The two lists cannot disagree, but the duplication is avoidable: `sessions_without_bars` could return the judged set and the missing set in one pass. Minor, but it is the kind of duplicated predicate that drifts.

findings.title: `bar_timestamp` catches `OverflowError` but `datetime.fromtimestamp` can also raise `OSError` on some platforms
findings.description: The tuple `(ValueError, TypeError, OverflowError)` matches `_bar_to_row`'s handling for the same field, and the comment explains the intent, but on some platforms `datetime.fromtimestamp` raises `OSError` for out-of-range values. `_bar_to_row` has the same gap (pre-existing), so this is consistent with the surrounding code rather than a new inconsistency — worth noting only if the two are ever unified.

findings.title: The `mt-minute-pass.timer` comment still describes the old staggering rationale
findings.description: The comment says "Staggered 30 minutes behind mt-daily-pass.timer", but the daily pass fires at 00:35/12:35 and the minute pass now at 04:05/13:05 — the offset is 3.5 h and 30 min, not 30 minutes. The `mt-kalshi-pass.timer` comment was updated to the new times (`04:05/13:05`) in this same change, so the minute timer's own rationale line was left behind.

findings.title: The firing-time constant, the timer unit, and the drift guard moved together
findings.description: `MINUTE_PASS_FIRING_TIMES_UTC` changed to `(time(4, 5), time(13, 5))`, `deploy/systemd/mt-minute-pass.timer` changed to the matching `OnCalendar` lines, and `test/unit/deploy/test_units.py::TestMinutePassTimerMatchesTheConstant` asserts both directions of agreement (every constant firing appears in the timer; the timer declares nothing the constant does not know; the counts match). The unit test in `test/unit/test_constants.py` was updated to the same value. The health check's `collecting_firing_finished_at` reads the constant rather than restating it, and its docstring, the `07:05` boundary, and `test_data_health.py` were all updated consistently — the derivation (20:00 close → next 04:05 firing → +3 h lag → 07:05) holds for both regular and early closes, and the "falls between the 13:05 and the following 04:05 firing" reasoning is correct.

findings.title: The session-judgement predicate agrees with the repair's truncation predicate
findings.description: The daemon judges a session collected only when a bar lands in `(open, close]`, and the repair's `find_truncated_days` calls a day truncated when `max(time) <= session_open_utc`. These are complementary halves of one predicate: a stored bar at or before the open means not collected; a bar strictly after the open and at or before the close means collected. The module docstring states this explicitly rather than restating the rule independently, and `test_minute_sessions.py` pins each boundary (bar at the open does not satisfy, bar at the close does, a bar one minute in does).

findings.title: The removal of the four-day trailing-weekend tolerance is covered by a behaviour test
findings.description: The old `_latest_bar_dt` + four-day tolerance was a heuristic; the replacement is session-based. The tests cover the weekend-tail case explicitly (`test_last_bar_before_the_chunk_end_is_still_success` and `test_all_sessions_covered_promotes_partial_to_success`), the spillover-only case, and the fully-covered case, and assert the resulting `fetch_status` passed to `_advance_minute_gap` — so the row-deletion behaviour is pinned, not just the returned enum.

findings.title: The unit tests for the cutover script now block subprocess, file writes, and sleeping
findings.description: The `_no_side_effects` autouse fixture patches `cutover_common.subprocess.run` to raise, pins `_LOG_FILE` to None, patches `start_log` to a tmp path, and patches both `time.sleep` seams. This directly addresses the stated incident ("an un-patched seam ran `sudo mt-run minute` from pytest"), and the `_verify_when_fresh` polling tests assert the poll count is bounded (`VERIFY_WAIT_POLLS + 1`) rather than merely that it terminates.

findings.title: The cagg freshness verdict is a pure, well-tested function with an explicit indeterminate-is-stale rule
findings.description: `CaggFreshness.stale` treats "no refresh on record" as stale when bars exist, and "no bars at all" as not stale — both pinned by tests in `test_repair_921.py::TestVerifyWaitsForTheCagg`, including the case where the probe reads the job stats and the session chunk with bound parameters (no string-built SQL).
